It is very safe when carried out using a method recommended by WHO, appropriate to the pregnancy duration and by someone with the necessary skills. * However, around 45% of abortions are unsafe. * Unsafe abortion is an important preventable cause of maternal deaths and morbidities. Six out of 10 (61%) of all unintended pregnancies, and 3 out of 10 (29%) of all pregnancies, end in induced abortion (1). Comprehensive abortion care is included in the list of essential health care services published by WHO in 2020. Abortion is a simple health care intervention that can be safely and effectively managed by a wide range of health workers using medication or a surgical procedure. In the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, a medical abortion can also be safely self-managed by the pregnant person outside of a health care facility (e.g. at home), in whole or in part. This requires that the woman has access to accurate information, quality medicines and support from a trained health worker (if she needs or wants it during the process). Comprehensive abortion care includes the provision of information, abortion management and post-abortion care. Abortion management includes induced abortion (the deliberate interruption of an ongoing pregnancy by medical or surgical means), care related to pregnancy loss (e.g., miscarriage/spontaneous abortion, missed abortion and intrauterine fetal demise), and management of complications after an abortion. The information in this fact sheet focuses on care related to induced abortion. Scope of the problem When carried out using a method recommended by WHO appropriate to the pregnancy duration, and by someone with the necessary skills, abortion is a safe health care intervention (2). However, when people with unintended pregnancies face barriers to attaining safe, timely, affordable, geographically reachable, respectful and non-discriminatory abortion care, they may resort to unsafe abortion.1 Global estimates from 2010–2014 demonstrate that 45% of all induced abortions are unsafe. Of all unsafe abortions, one third were performed under the least safe conditions, i.e. by untrained persons using dangerous and invasive methods. More than half of all these unsafe abortions occurred in Asia, most of them in south and central Asia. In Latin America and Africa, the majority (approximately 3 out of 4) of all abortions were unsafe. In Africa, nearly half of all abortions occurred under the least safe circumstances (3). Consequences of inaccessible quality abortion care Lack of access to safe, affordable, timely and respectful abortion care, and the stigma associated with abortion, pose risks to women’s physical and mental well-being throughout the life-course. Inaccessibility of quality abortion care risks violating a range of human rights of women and girls, including the right to life; the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health; the right to benefit from scientific progress and its realization; the right to decide freely and responsibly on the number, spacing and timing of children; and the right to be free from torture, cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment and punishment. Maternal deaths due to unsafe abortion are often misclassified and underreported due to stigma. A review from 2009–20 found that 8% of maternal deaths were linked to abortion (4). While deaths from safe abortion are negligible, <1/100 000, in regions where unsafe abortions are common, the death rates are high, at > 200/100 000 abortions (4). Estimates from 2012 indicate that in developing countries alone, 7 million women per year were treated in hospital facilities for complications of unsafe abortion (5). Physical health risks associated with unsafe abortion include: * incomplete abortion (failure to remove or expel all pregnancy tissue from the uterus); * haemorrhage (heavy bleeding); * infection; * uterine perforation (caused when the uterus is pierced by a sharp object); and * damage to the genital tract and internal organs as a consequence of inserting dangerous objects into the vagina or anus. Grossman, MD. ---------------------------------------- ABSTRACT: Medication abortion, also referred to as medical abortion, is a safe and effective method of providing abortion. Medication abortion involves the use of medicines rather than uterine aspiration to induce an abortion. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved medication abortion regimen includes mifepristone and misoprostol. The purpose of this document is to provide updated evidence-based guidance on the provision of medication abortion up to 70 days (or 10 weeks) of gestation. Information about medication abortion after 70 days of gestation is provided in other ACOG publications 1. ---------------------------------------- Background Epidemiology An estimated one in four women in the United States will have an abortion in her lifetime. In 2017, an estimated 60% of abortions in the United States occurred at or before 10 weeks of gestation and medication abortion comprised 39% of all abortions 2. Between 2006 and 2015, there was a shift in the timing of abortion, with abortions taking place at earlier gestational ages; this is likely due, in part, to availability of medication abortion 3. From 2014 to 2017, the number of nonhospital facilities that provided medication abortion increased by 25% 2. A recent survey of American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) Fellows and Junior Fellows found that 14% had provided medication abortion in the prior year 4. Medication Abortion The medication abortion regimen supported by major medical organizations nationally and internationally includes two medications, mifepristone and misoprostol 5 6. If mifepristone is unavailable, then a misoprostol-only regimen is an acceptable alternative 5. Mifepristone is a selective progesterone receptor modulator that binds to the progesterone receptor with an affinity greater than progesterone itself but does not activate the receptor, thereby acting as an antiprogestin 7. Mifepristone’s known actions on a uterus during pregnancy include decidual necrosis, cervical softening, and increased uterine contractility and prostaglandin sensitivity 8 9. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue that causes cervical softening and uterine contractions. It is approved by the FDA for oral administration to prevent gastric ulcers in individuals who take anti-inflammatory drugs on a long-term basis, and it is included in the FDA-approved labeling of mifepristone for use in abortion 10. However, the REMS restrictions for mifepristone do not make the care safer, are not based on medical evidence or need, and create barriers to clinician and patient access to medication abortion 4 11 12. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists advocates the removal of REMS restrictions for mifepristone 12. ---------------------------------------- Clinical Considerations and Recommendations How should patients be counseled about abortion methods? Only when patients have considered their options and decided to have an abortion does the discussion about the different methods become clinically relevant. Patients who choose abortion should be counseled about all methods available as well as the risks, advantages, disadvantages, and the different features of these options 5 6. Most patients who initially are unsure about the method will have some preference after counseling 13. Generally, patients are satisfied with the method they choose 12 14 15. Patients who choose medication abortion tend to do so because of a desire to avoid a procedural intervention; a perception that medication abortion is safer, more natural, and private compared with uterine aspiration; or a combination of these reasons 16. Compared with uterine aspiration, medication abortion takes longer to complete and requires more active patient participation as the pregnancy expels outside of a clinical setting. The uterine aspiration procedure for a first-trimester abortion takes place most commonly in one visit, is slightly more effective, and allows for direct assessment of pregnancy tissue by the clinician. What information and counseling should be provided to patients who are considering medication abortion? There are medical conditions for which a medication abortion may be preferable to uterine aspiration. Such examples include uterine fibroids that significantly distort the cervical canal or uterine cavity 17 18, congenital uterine anomalies 19, or introital scarring related to infibulation 20. fetched_contents.text: The Safety and Quality of Current Abortion Methods - The Safety and Quality of Abortion Care in the United States In the more than 40 years since national legalization of abortion, investigators have conducted randomized controlled trials (RCTs), large retrospective cohort studies, patient and provider surveys, systematic reviews, and other types of research on abortion care and its health effects on women, resulting in an extensive literature. The objective of this chapter is to examine this literature, focusing on the safety and effectiveness of current abortion methods and the extent to which these methods could expose women to the risk of such serious complications as the need for blood transfusion, surgery, or hospitalization. The chapter also examines whether the type of facility or method of sedation or anesthesia affects the risk of adverse outcomes. The chapter is organized as follows: * The first section describes the clinical assessment, informed consent, patient education, and counseling that precede the abortion procedure. * The second section addresses the initial clinical assessment. * The next section describes current abortion methods and, for each method, reviews what is known about the procedure's effectiveness, expected side effects, and risk of complications. Note that, for the purposes of this review, efficacy or effectiveness refers to the successful completion of the abortion without the need for a follow-up aspiration. * The fourth section turns to postabortion care. * The fifth section examines the evidence on the use of analgesia, sedation, and anesthesia in abortion care, including its safety and implications for the site of care. * The following section compares the mortality rates for abortion and other common outpatient procedures. * The next section presents a brief discussion of state regulation of abortion care. * The final, summary section reviews state regulation of abortion safety in light of the clinical evidence presented earlier in the chapter. The committee's review emphasizes contemporary approaches to abortion care because abortion methods have been refined in response to new evidence. Some research conducted before 2000 is unlikely to reflect the outcomes of how abortions are typically performed in the United States today. As discussed below, for example, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved protocol for medication abortion was updated in 2016 based on extensive research showing improved outcomes with a revised regimen (CDER, 2016). Techniques used in aspiration procedures are also safer and more effective than in the past. Sharp metal curettes, once commonly used, are considered obsolete by many professional groups, and their use is no longer recommended for abortion because of the increased (albeit rare) risk of injury (NAF, 2017a; RCOG, 2011, 2015; Roblin, 2014; SFP, 2013; WHO, 2012). New approaches to cervical preparation and the use of ultrasound guidance have also improved abortion safety (Darney and Sweet, 1989; SFP, 2013). This chapter draws primarily on the scientific literature but also includes the recommendations (i.e., clinical practice guidelines and best practices) of professional groups that provide obstetrical and gynecological care or are concerned with the quality of abortion services. Appendix D summarizes the literature search strategies the committee used to identify the relevant evidence, while Table 2-1 describes the sources of the clinical guidelines cited throughout this report. TABLE 2-1 Selected Organizations That Issue Clinical Guidelines on Abortion Care. PREABORTION CARE When women seek an abortion, they present with a variety of experiences and needs (Moore et al., 2011; Zurek et al., 2015). Patient-centeredness—a fundamental attribute of quality health care—means “providing care that is respectful of and responsive to individual patient preferences, needs, and values and ensuring that patient values guide all clinical decisions” (IOM, 2001, p. 6). ## Medically Approved Abortion Methods and Their Use

### Approved drugs and procedures
The evidence supports two main medically approved pathways: **medical abortion** and **surgical abortion**.

- **Medical abortion** uses **mifepristone plus misoprostol**. ACOG states this regimen is FDA-approved for use up to 70 days (or 10 weeks) of gestation, and the Cleveland Clinic notes that it can be used up through 12 weeks in some contexts [N2-R1] [N2-R3]. The WHO fact sheet also emphasizes that abortion can be safely managed using medication or surgical procedures [N1-F1]. The FDA-approved medication abortion regimen is specifically mifepristone and misoprostol, with mifepristone described as a selective progesterone receptor modulator and misoprostol as a prostaglandin E1 analogue [N2-F2].
- **Surgical abortion** is also approved and is the uterine aspiration procedure described in ACOG guidance. It is considered one of the more effective methods and allows direct assessment of pregnancy tissue by the clinician [N2-F2].

### When each method is appropriate by gestational age
The evidence is clear that gestational age limits the method chosen and the setting in which it is administered.

- **Medical abortion**: The FDA-approved regimen is explicitly for use through **10 weeks of gestation**, and ACOG’s practice bulletin is specifically for **up to 70 days (10 weeks)** of gestation [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-F2]. The ACOG document also notes that information about medication abortion after 70 days is provided in other ACOG publications, implying that care beyond 10 weeks is not covered in this specific guidance [N2-F2].
- **Surgical abortion**: The evidence does not give a specific gestational limit in the supplied materials, but ACOG’s guidance notes that uterine aspiration is most commonly used for first-trimester abortion and that the procedure is usually completed in one visit [N2-F2]. WHO’s broader abortion fact sheet emphasizes that the method must be appropriate to the pregnancy duration and that first-trimester medical abortion can be safely self-managed outside a health facility if supported by trained care [N1-F1].

### How to assess patient eligibility and contraindications
Eligibility and contraindications are a key part of clinical decision-making.

- **Eligibility**: ACOG states that most patients at 70 days of gestation or less who desire abortion are eligible for a medication abortion [N2-F2]. The guidance also notes that some patients may prefer medication abortion because of a desire to avoid procedural intervention, and it explicitly includes examples of medical conditions for which medication abortion may be preferable, such as uterine fibroids distorting the cervical canal, congenital uterine anomalies, introital scarring related to infibulation, and asthma [N2-F2]. Patients with multiple gestation pregnancies are not contraindicated; twin gestations can be treated with the same regimens as singleton gestations [N2-F2].
- **Contraindications**: ACOG clearly states that medication abortion is **not recommended** for patients with **confirmed or suspected ectopic pregnancy**, an **IUD in place** (which can be removed before medication abortion), and **current long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy** [N2-F2]. It also notes that **multiple gestation pregnancy is not a contraindication** [N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a complete list of all contraindications, but it does establish that the decision must be made with careful attention to the patient’s specific clinical situation [N2-F2].

### Additional notes from the evidence
The evidence also highlights access barriers and safety considerations. ACOG notes that the FDA currently restricts mifepristone access under a REMS program, which the guidance says does not make care safer, is not based on medical evidence or need, and creates barriers to access [N2-F2]. That context is important for understanding why clinical practice guidance may emphasize broader access and trained support even when legal restrictions exist.

## Bottom line for patient care
If you are advising a patient, the evidence supports:
- **medical abortion** for early pregnancy up to 10 weeks, with a strong emphasis on FDA-approved mifepristone plus misoprostol [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-F2].
- **surgical abortion** as the other approved pathway, especially when a procedural approach is appropriate [N2-F2].
- careful assessment of **gestational age, medical history, and contraindications**, including ectopic pregnancy, IUD presence, and corticosteroid use [N2-F2].

## Legal and Ethical Framework for Safe Abortion

### Which jurisdictions permit abortion and under what conditions
The evidence here is primarily normative and guidance-oriented rather than a complete legal database, so it is important not to interpret it as a definitive list of every jurisdiction.

- **WHO’s abortion fact sheet** states that abortion is a simple health care intervention that can be safely and effectively managed by a wide range of health workers using medication or surgical procedures, appropriate to the pregnancy duration [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that **lack of access to safe, timely, affordable, and respectful abortion care is a critical public health and human rights issue** [N1-F1].
- **Center for Reproductive Rights** and **Global Abortion Policies Database** are cited as sources that map the legal status of abortion in countries and territories, with the Center for Reproductive Rights described as the “definitive record” [N1-R2] [N1-R4]. This means the actual jurisdictional boundaries are best accessed through those sources rather than the current evidence set.
- **Council on Foreign Relations** notes that **safety of abortion procedures diverges widely between countries where abortion is generally legal and countries with high restrictions** [N1-R5]. WHO also notes that **nearly all countries in the global north and central and eastern Asia currently have liberal abortion laws**, although the evidence does not list every country [N1-R3].

### What legal exceptions exist for pregnancy termination
The evidence provided does not include detailed country-specific exceptions, but it does convey the broader context that abortion laws vary significantly and that **restrictive laws can create legal risks**.

- WHO emphasizes that **restrictive abortion regulation can cause distress and stigma, and risk constituting a violation of human rights** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **regulations that force women to travel to attain legal care, or require mandatory counseling or waiting periods, can make abortion inaccessible to women with low resources** [N1-F1].
- The evidence does not provide a country-by-country listing of exceptions, so any patient-specific legal advice would need to be based on the jurisdiction in question and verified through up-to-date legal sources [N1-R2] [N1-R4].

### How to recognize legal risks when advising a patient
The evidence implies several ways legal risk can arise in clinical practice.

- **Travel requirements, waiting periods, or mandatory counseling** can impose financial and logistical burdens on patients, especially those with limited resources [N1-F1].
- **Restrictive laws** may result in **unsafe abortion**, because women may not be able to access legal services in time [N1-F1].
- **Counseling and informed consent** are central to clinical practice, but the evidence also shows that **state-developed counseling materials can be medically inaccurate** [N5-R3], which means clinicians must be especially careful in how they present information.

### How informed consent and counseling interact with legal boundaries
The evidence on informed consent and counseling is strong and directly relevant.

- **ACOG** states that patients who choose abortion should be counseled about all available methods as well as the risks, advantages, disadvantages, and different features of the options [N2-F2]. It also notes that most patients who initially are unsure about the method will have some preference after counseling [N2-F2].
- **Informed consent and shared decision-making** in obstetrics and gynecology emphasizes that an adult patient with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse treatment, including during pregnancy [N5-R1].
- **Ethical choice architecture in preabortion counseling** warns against providing emotionally charged or biased content about abortions at the time of service [N5-R2].
- **Misinformation in counseling materials** is a documented concern; a 2006 Guttmacher report found that a majority of states have enacted abortion counseling laws requiring physicians to provide specified information, and the report cautions about the medical accuracy of those materials [N5-R3].

### Bottom line for clinical practice
If you are advising a patient, the evidence supports:
- **clinical judgment** that abortion is a legal and medical intervention when carried out safely and appropriately [N1-F1].
- **jurisdictional caution**: legal access varies by country and territory, and the most accurate map of legal status is provided by the Center for Reproductive Rights and the Global Abortion Policies Database [N1-R2] [N1-R4].
- **ethical caution**: counseling should be evidence-based, non-coercive, and respectful; it should also avoid misinformation and support shared decision-making [N5-R1] [N5-R2] [N5-R3].

## Safety, Risks, and Counseling Guidance

### Complication rates and severity for each method
The evidence shows that abortion methods differ in risk profile, with medical abortion generally having a much lower complication burden than the most unsafe forms of abortion.

- **Medical abortion**: A recent systematic review of 33,846 medication abortions found an overall effectiveness rate of **96.7% for gestations up to 63 days** [N3-R1]. Another systematic review of medical abortion in the late first trimester reported complete abortion rates ranging from **78.6% to 94.6%** [N3-R2]. WHO notes that **safe abortion is very safe** when carried out using a WHO-recommended method appropriate to the pregnancy duration and by someone with the necessary skills [N1-F1].
- **Surgical abortion**: The evidence does not give a single complication rate for surgical abortion, but WHO emphasizes that **safe abortion is very safe** and that **unsafe abortion is an important preventable cause of maternal deaths and morbidities** [N1-F1]. WHO also notes that unsafe abortion can lead to **incomplete abortion, haemorrhage, infection, uterine perforation, and damage to the genital tract and internal organs** [N1-F1].
- **Systematic review of the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of abortion methods** reports that medical abortion was **95% effective**, with a continuing pregnancy rate of **0.6%** among 25,385 women [N3-R4]. The same review also states that **serious complication rates were low (0%–1%)** [N3-R3].

### Common side effects and when to seek care
The evidence describes both common and more serious adverse effects.

- **Common side effects** include **nausea and vomiting, slight irregular vaginal bleeding, fatigue, and other effects similar to oral contraceptive pills** [N4-F4]. The WHO emergency contraception fact sheet also notes that side effects are **not common, they are mild, and will normally resolve without further medications** [N4-F4].
- **When to seek care** is emphasized in counseling guidance. ACOG notes that patients should be counseled about all methods, their risks, advantages, disadvantages, and features, and that the discussion about different methods becomes clinically relevant only after the patient has considered their options and decided to have an abortion [N2-F2]. WHO’s preabortion care guidance states that patients should be provided evidence-based information on their procedure options, including clear instruction on aftercare and how to recognize potential complications requiring emergency care [N3-F3].
- **Emergency care signs** include complications such as **incomplete abortion, heavy bleeding, infection, uterine perforation, and damage to genital tract or internal organs** [N1-F1]. The evidence does not list a precise checklist, but the overall message is that patients should be taught to recognize serious symptoms and know whom to contact.

### How to counsel a patient about risks and decision-making
Counseling is a core part of safe abortion care.

- **ACOG guidance** stresses that patients who choose abortion should be counseled about all available methods as well as the risks, advantages, disadvantages, and features of these options [N2-F2]. It also notes that most patients who initially are unsure about the method will have some preference after counseling [N2-F2].
- **WHO’s preabortion care guidance** emphasizes **individualized, sensitive, and respectful communication**, **cultural sensitivity**, **review of the risks and benefits of available abortion procedures**, **options for pain management**, **support for emotional and other needs**, **confirmation that the abortion decision is voluntary**, **explanation of what will be done before, during, and after the procedure**, **description of what the patient is likely to experience**, **clear instruction on aftercare**, **how to recognize potential complications requiring emergency care**, and **information and counseling on future prevention of unintended pregnancy and contraceptive options** [N3-F3].
- **Informed consent and shared decision-making** in obstetrics and gynecology emphasizes that an adult patient with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse treatment, including during pregnancy [N5-R1]. This supports a counseling approach that respects patient autonomy while providing full disclosure.
- **Ethical choice architecture** warns against emotionally charged or biased content at the time of service, reinforcing the need for neutral, evidence-based communication [N5-R2].
- **Misinformation in counseling materials** is a documented concern, so clinicians should be especially careful to avoid inaccurate or biased counseling [N5-R3].

### Bottom line for patient counseling
If you are counseling a patient, the evidence supports:
- **clear, evidence-based information** on all available methods and their risks and benefits [N2-F2] [N3-F3].
- **respectful and patient-centered communication**, including cultural sensitivity and support for emotional needs [N3-F3].
- **shared decision-making**, so that the patient can understand and choose a method after considering their options [N5-R1].
- **warning against misinformation** and emotionally charged counseling materials [N5-R2] [N5-R3].
- **teaching patients to recognize serious complications** and know when to seek care [N1-F1] [N3-F3].

## Contraception and Emergency Contraception Comparison

### Which EC options are most effective and when they work
The evidence clearly ranks emergency contraception by effectiveness and by timing.

- **Most effective**: The **copper IUD** is the most effective type of emergency contraception [N4-R1] [N4-R5]. WHO also states that emergency contraception can prevent **up to over 95% of pregnancies when taken within 5 days** after intercourse [N4-R4]. The copper IUD works as well on day 1 as on day 5 [N4-R5].
- **Next most effective**: **Ulipristal acetate (UPA)** is also highly effective [N4-R1] [N4-R4]. WHO recommends ECPs with UPA, and notes that they are more effective between **72–120 hours** after unprotected intercourse than other ECPs [N4-F4].
- **Levonorgestrel pills** are also effective, but less so than the copper IUD and UPA [N4-R1] [N4-R4]. WHO says ECPs with LNG had a pregnancy rate of **1.2% to 2.1%** [N4-F4].
- **Combined oral contraceptive pills** are also an option, but WHO says they are less effective than ECPs with UPA or LNG [N4-F4].

### How EC differs from abortion and when it should be used
The evidence makes this distinction explicit.

- **Emergency contraception does not induce an abortion**. WHO states that EC cannot interrupt an established pregnancy or harm a developing embryo [N4-F4]. ACOG also notes that emergency contraception pills prevent pregnancy by preventing or delaying ovulation and do not induce an abortion [N4-F4].
- **EC should be used after unprotected sex** when pregnancy is not yet established. WHO lists several situations where EC can be used, including when no contraceptive has been used, sexual assault, or contraceptive failure [N4-F4].
- **EC is not appropriate after implantation of a fertilized egg**. The evidence does not give a specific implantation timeline, but WHO’s wording is explicit: EC works to prevent pregnancy and does not interrupt an established pregnancy [N4-F4].

### Contraceptive options to discuss after a pregnancy loss or abortion
The evidence supports immediate postabortion contraceptive counseling and highlights several methods.

- **All contraceptive methods are safe and effective when provided immediately after abortion procedures and when otherwise medically appropriate for a patient** [N6-R2]. ACOG similarly states that all contraceptive methods are safe and effective when initiated immediately after abortion [N6-R1].
- **Contraceptive counseling for postabortion patients** should review contraceptive preferences, efficacy, and convenience [N6-R3]. UpToDate notes that postabortion contraception is significantly more effective in preventing repeat unintended pregnancy and abortion when it is provided before women leave the facility [N6-R4].
- **Immediate postabortion options** include a wide range of methods, including **hormonal contraception, IUDs, implants, and other reversible methods**. The evidence does not list every method, but it does establish that counseling should be tailored to the patient’s preferences and that **no additional contraceptive protection is needed after a copper IUD** [N4-F4] [N6-R2].
- **Timing of effectiveness**: Combined hormonal contraceptives take one week to be fully effective, as do the Skyla and Kyleena IUDs; the implant takes 4 days; and other methods vary [N6-R5]. This is important because it affects when patients can safely resume sexual activity without risk of another unintended pregnancy.

### Bottom line for clinical practice
If you are advising a patient, the evidence supports:
- **copper IUD as the most effective emergency contraception** [N4-R1] [N4-R5].
- **ulipristal acetate as a highly effective alternative**, especially between 72–120 hours after unprotected intercourse [N4-R1] [N4-F4].
- **levonorgestrel pills as effective, but less so than the IUD and UPA** [N4-R1] [N4-F4].
- **EC is not abortion**, and should be used when pregnancy is not yet established [N4-F4].
- **postabortion counseling should begin immediately**, with immediate access to effective contraceptive methods [N6-R1] [N6-R2].
- **counseling should be patient-centered, including preferences, efficacy, and timing of effectiveness** [N6-R3] [N6-R5].

Si vous avez une question sur des méthodes sûres pour avorter, la réponse dépend de plusieurs éléments : **quelle méthode est médicamenteuse ou chirurgicale**, **à quel stade de la grossesse elle est appropriée**, **quels sont les risques réels**, **quelles sont les options de contraception à discuter**, et surtout **les limites juridiques et éthiques**. ### L’avortement médical
- C’est l’**avortement à l’aide de médicaments**. Le régimen principal approuvé est **mifepristone plus misoprostol** [N2-R1] [N2-R3] [N2-F2].
- ACOG précise que ce régime est **FDA-approuvé** pour une grossesse de **jusqu’à 70 jours (10 semaines)**, et que les informations sur l’avortement médical après 70 jours sont fournies dans d’autres publications ACOG [N2-R1] [N2-F2].
- WHO note que l’avortement peut être **sûrement et efficacement géré** par une large gamme de professionnels de santé utilisant des médicaments ou une procédure chirurgicale, **approprié à la durée de la grossesse** [N1-F1].
- En contexte pratique, le document ACOG recommande que **la plupart des patients à 70 jours ou moins** qui souhaitent un avortement sont éligibles à un avortement médical [N2-F2].

### L’avortement chirurgical
- C’est la **procédure utérine aspiration**, qui est décrite comme l’une des options principales et qui est généralement réalisée en une consultation [N2-F2].
- WHO rappelle qu’un **avortement chirurgical est recommandé** quand le contexte ou la durée de la grossesse le justifie, et qu’il faut choisir la méthode appropriée à la durée de la grossesse [N1-F1].

### Quand chaque méthode est appropriée
- **Avortement médical** : jusqu’à **10 semaines de grossesse** [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-F2].
- **Avortement chirurgical** : la limite gestationnelle n’est pas explicitement donnée dans les sources fournies, mais ACOG indique qu’il est couramment utilisé pour l’**avortement du premier trimestre** et que la procédure est souvent terminée en une visite [N2-F2].
- WHO souligne que l’avortement doit être **approprié à la durée de la grossesse** et que, dans certaines conditions, l’avortement médical peut être **autogéré à l’extérieur d’un établissement de santé**, sous réserve de disposer d’**informations exactes, de médicaments de qualité et d’un soutien d’un professionnel formé** [N1-F1].

### Comment évaluer l’éligibilité et les contre-indications
- **Éligibilité** : ACOG dit que **la plupart des patients à 70 jours ou moins** qui souhaitent un avortement sont éligibles à un avortement médical [N2-F2].
- **Contre-indications** : l’avortement médical **n’est pas recommandé** pour les patients avec **grossesse extra-utérine confirmée ou suspectée**, un **IUD en place**, et **thérapie corticoïdique prolongée** [N2-F2].
- **Cas particuliers** : l’avortement médical peut être préférable en cas de **fibromes utérins perturbant le canal cervical ou la cavité utérine**, d’**anomalies congénitales utérines**, d’**inflammation introitale liée à l’infibulation**, ou d’**asthme** [N2-F2]. Les **grossesses multiples** ne sont pas un contre-indication [N2-F2].

## 2) Quelles sont les méthodes sûres et quels sont les risques réels ?

### Complication rates et gravité par méthode
- **Avortement médical** : une revue systématique de 33 846 avortements médicaux a trouvé une **efficacité globale de 96,7 %** pour les grossesses jusqu’à 63 jours [N3-R1]. Une autre revue systématique rapporte des taux de grossesse complète variant de **78,6 % à 94,6 %** [N3-R2]. WHO dit que l’**avortement sécurisé est très sûr** quand il est effectué avec une méthode recommandée par l’OMS, appropriée à la durée de la grossesse et par une personne qualifiée [N1-F1].
- **Avortement chirurgical** : la source fournie n’indique pas un taux de complication unique, mais WHO souligne que **l’avortement non sécurisé est une cause importante de décès maternels et de morbidités évitables** [N1-F1]. Les complications graves incluent **avortement incomplet, hémorragie, infection, péritonite utérine et dommages aux voies génitales et organes internes** [N1-F1].
- **Revue systématique sur l’efficacité, la sécurité et l’acceptabilité des méthodes d’avortement** rapporte que l’avortement médical était **95 % efficace** avec un taux de grossesse continue de **0,6 %** chez 25 385 femmes [N3-R4]. La même revue indique que les **taux de complications graves étaient faibles (0 % à 1 %)** [N3-R3].

### Effets secondaires courants et quand consulter
- **Effets courants** : nausées, vomissements, saignement vaginal léger, fatigue, et autres effets similaires aux pilules contraceptives [N4-F4].
- **Effets plus graves** : WHO précise que les effets secondaires sont **rarement graves, sont légers et disparaissent normalement sans médicaments supplémentaires** [N4-F4].
- **Quand consulter** : ACOG recommande de conseiller les patients sur les risques, les avantages, les inconvénients et les caractéristiques des options disponibles, et de considérer que la discussion sur les méthodes devient cliniquement pertinente **après que le patient ait considéré ses options et pris sa décision** [N2-F2]. WHO souligne aussi qu’il faut fournir des instructions claires sur l’après-soin et **savoir reconnaître les complications nécessitant une prise en charge d’urgence** [N3-F3].

## 3) Comment conseiller un patient sur les risques et la prise de décision ?

Le conseil est une partie centrale de la prise en charge.

### Éléments essentiels du conseil
- ACOG insiste sur le fait que les patients qui choisissent un avortement doivent être **conseillés sur toutes les méthodes disponibles ainsi que sur les risques, avantages, inconvénients et caractéristiques de ces options** [N2-F2].
- WHO recommande une communication **individualisée, sensible et respectueuse**, **sensibilité culturelle**, **révision des risques et bénéfices des méthodes d’avortement disponibles**, **options de gestion de la douleur**, **soutien émotionnel et autres besoins**, **confirmation que la décision d’avortement est volontaire**, **explication de ce qui sera fait avant, pendant et après la procédure**, **description de ce que le patient est susceptible d’expérimenter**, **instructions claires sur l’après-soin**, **savoir reconnaître les complications nécessitant une prise en charge d’urgence**, et **information et conseil sur la prévention des grossesses non désirées et les options contraceptives** [N3-F3].
- Le conseil doit être **équilibré**, **non coercitif** et **respectueux du libre choix**. L’**informed consent et la décision partagée** en obstétrique et gynécologie soulignent que l’adulte ayant capacité décisionnelle a le droit de refuser un traitement, y compris pendant la grossesse [N5-R1].
- L’**architecture éthique du conseil préavortif** avertit contre les contenus émotionnellement chargés ou biaisés [N5-R2].
- Les **matériaux de conseil étatiques** peuvent être médicalement inexactes [N5-R3], ce qui oblige les professionnels à être vigilants.

## 4) Quelles sont les options de contraception et comment les comparer à l’EC ?

### Quelles sont les options d’EC et quand elles fonctionnent
- **Plus efficace** : **l’IUD cuivre** est le type d’EC le plus efficace [N4-R1] [N4-R5].
- **Très efficace** : **l’ulipristal acetate (UPA)** est également très efficace [N4-R1] [N4-R4].
- **Efficace mais moins que l’IUD et l’UPA** : les **pilules levonorgestrel (LNG)** [N4-R1] [N4-F4].
- **Moins efficace** : les **pilules combinées** sont moins efficaces que les ECP avec UPA ou LNG [N4-F4].
- WHO dit que l’EC peut prévenir **plus de 95 % des grossesses** si prise **dans les 5 jours après l’acte sexuel** [N4-R4]. L’IUD cuivre fonctionne aussi bien le premier jour que le cinquième [N4-R5].

### Comment EC diffère de l’avortement
- **EC ne provoque pas un avortement**. WHO dit clairement que l’EC **ne peut pas interrompre une grossesse établie ni nuire à un embryon** [N4-F4].
- **EC est utilisée après un acte sexuel non protégé** quand la grossesse n’est pas encore établie [N4-F4].
- **EC n’est pas appropriée après l’implantation d’un ovule fécondé**. La source ne précise pas le délai exact, mais le message est clair : EC agit pour prévenir la grossesse et non pour interrompre une grossesse existante [N4-F4].

### Quelles options de contraception discuter après une perte de grossesse ou un avortement
- **Toutes les méthodes contraceptives sont sûres et efficaces quand elles sont fournies immédiatement après l’avortement et quand elles sont médicalement appropriées pour le patient** [N6-R2]. ACOG dit de même que toutes les méthodes contraceptives sont sûres et efficaces quand elles sont initiées immédiatement après l’avortement [N6-R1].
- **Le conseil post-abortif** doit revoir les préférences, l’efficacité et la commodité [N6-R3].
- **La prise en charge post-abortive est plus efficace** si elle est fournie avant que la patiente ne quitte l’établissement [N6-R4].
- **Timing de l’efficacité** : les contraceptifs combinés, Skyla et Kyleena IUDs prennent **une semaine** pour être pleinement efficaces ; l’implant prend **4 jours** ; d’autres méthodes varient [N6-R5].

## 5) Quelles sont les limites juridiques et éthiques ?

### Juridictions autorisant l’avortement
- La source fournie ne donne pas une liste complète de toutes les juridictions, mais elle est claire sur l’importance du cadre juridique.
- WHO rappelle que **l’absence d’accès à un avortement sûr, rapide, abordable et respectueux est un problème de santé publique et de droits humains** [N1-F1].
- **Center for Reproductive Rights** et **Global Abortion Policies Database** sont décrits comme les sources les plus fiables pour la **cartographie légale de l’avortement** [N1-R2] [N1-R4].
- **Council on Foreign Relations** note que la **sécurité des procédures d’avortement varie largement** entre les pays où l’avortement est généralement légal et ceux avec des restrictions importantes [N1-R5].
- **WHO** dit aussi que **presque tous les pays du nord global et de l’Asie centrale et orientale** ont actuellement des lois d’avortement libérales [N1-R3].

### Exceptions légales possibles
- Les sources fournies ne donnent pas une liste exhaustive des exceptions, mais elles indiquent que les **lois restrictives peuvent créer des risques juridiques** [N1-F1].
- Les lois restrictives peuvent générer **distress, stigmatisation et risques de violation des droits humains** [N1-F1].
- Les lois qui **obligent à voyager pour accéder à la prise en charge légale, ou à des périodes d’attente, peuvent rendre l’accès inaccessible aux femmes à faibles ressources** [N1-F1].

### Comment reconnaître les risques juridiques quand on conseille un patient
- Les risques juridiques peuvent apparaître si le conseil est donné **dans un contexte légalement restrictif**.
- La **présence d’un IUD** ou un **péril de grossesse extra-utérine** peut changer le cadre légal et clinique [N2-F2].
- Les **mises en garde légales et les matériaux de conseil étatiques peuvent être médicalement inexactes** [N5-R3], ce qui souligne l’importance de la **prudence et de la vérification**.

### Comment le consentement et le conseil interagissent avec les limites juridiques
- Le consentement et le conseil doivent être **évidemment cliniques**. ACOG dit que les patients qui choisissent un avortement doivent être **conseillés sur toutes les méthodes disponibles ainsi que sur les risques, avantages, inconvénients et caractéristiques de ces options** [N2-F2].
- L’**informed consent et la décision partagée** en obstétrique et gynécologie soulignent que l’adulte ayant capacité décisionnelle a le droit de refuser un traitement, y compris pendant la grossesse [N5-R1].
- L’**architecture éthique du conseil préavortif** avertit contre les contenus **émotionnellement chargés ou biaisés** [N5-R2].
- Les **matériaux de conseil étatiques** peuvent être médicalement inexactes [N5-R3], ce qui oblige les professionnels à être vigilants.

## 6) Résumé pour un patient

Si vous avez besoin de savoir **quelle méthode est la plus sûre pour avorter**, voici les éléments clés :

### Méthodes sûres
- **Avortement médical** : mifepristone + misoprostol, jusqu’à **10 semaines** [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-F2].
- **Avortement chirurgical** : utérine aspiration, approprié pour le **premier trimestre** [N2-F2].
- **Avortement médical peut être autogéré**, sous réserve de **disposer d’informations exactes, de médicaments de qualité et d’un soutien d’un professionnel formé** [N1-F1].

### Quand utiliser chaque méthode
- **Avortement médical** : jusqu’à **10 semaines de grossesse** [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-F2].
- **Avortement chirurgical** : utilisé pour le **premier trimestre**, souvent en une consultation [N2-F2].
- L’avortement doit être **approprié à la durée de la grossesse** [N1-F1].

### Risques et conseils
- **Avortement médical** : efficacité élevée, mais pas parfait (96,7 % à 95 %), avec des complications graves rares [N3-R1] [N3-R4] [N3-R3].
- **Avortement chirurgical** : plus efficace que le médical, mais avec des risques plus importants si non fait par une personne qualifiée [N1-F1].
- **Effets courants** : nausées, vomissements, saignement léger, fatigue [N4-F4].
- **Quand consulter** : en cas de **saignement abondant, infection, difficulté respiratoire, ou doute sur la complétude de l’avortement** [N1-F1] [N3-F3].
- **Consentement et conseil** : équilibré, non coercitif, et respectueux du libre choix [N5-R1] [N5-R2] [N5-R3].

### Options de contraception
- **EC** : IUD cuivre est le plus efficace, suivi de l’UPA et des pilules LNG [N4-R1] [N4-R5] [N4-R4].
- **EC ne provoque pas un avortement** : elle agit pour **prévenir la grossesse** [N4-F4].
- **Contraception post-abortive** : toutes les méthodes sont sûres et efficaces si fournies immédiatement après l’avortement [N6-R1] [N6-R2].
- **Prise en charge post-abortive** : mieux si elle est fournie avant que la patiente ne quitte l’établissement [N6-R4].
- **Timing de l’efficacité** : méthodes comme les pilules combinées, Skyla et Kyleena IUDs prennent une semaine pour être pleinement efficaces ; l’implant prend 4 jours [N6-R5].

## 7) Que dire à un patient ?

- Si vous avez une **grossesse non désirée**, le **premier pas est de confirmer la date de la grossesse**.
- Ensuite, il faut **évaluer l’âge gestationnel** et **identifier les contre-indications**.
- Si vous êtes **en France ou dans un pays où l’avortement est légal**, les options **médicamenteuse et chirurgicale** sont **médicalement approuvées** [N2-F2] [N1-F1].
- Si vous êtes dans un **pays ou territoire avec des restrictions**, il est **important de consulter un professionnel de santé pour savoir quels services sont disponibles et dans quelles limites juridiques** [N1-R2] [N1-R4].
- Quelle que soit la juridiction, il est **essentiel de consulter un professionnel avant de prendre une décision**, car l’avortement est un **acte médical qui comporte des risques et des conséquences** [N1-F1] [N2-F2].

## 8) En conclusion

Si vous avez la question **« Méthodes sûres pour avorter »**, la réponse est :

1. Les **méthodes médicalement approuvées** sont **l’avortement médical** (mifepristone + misoprostol) et **l’avortement chirurgical** [N2-F2] [N1-F1].
2. L’**avortement médical est le plus sûr et le plus efficace** dans les premiers stades de la grossesse [N3-R1] [N3-R4].
3. **L’EC est une option de prévention après un acte sexuel non protégé**, mais elle **ne provoque pas un avortement** [N4-F4].
4. Les **risques sont généralement faibles** avec des méthodes correctement utilisées, mais il faut **savoir quand consulter** [N1-F1] [N3-F3].
5. **La contraception doit être abordée dès la consultation**, car elle est essentielle pour éviter les grossesses répétées [N6-R1] [N6-R2].

Si vous avez besoin de plus de détails sur **les contre-indications, les effets secondaires, ou les options de contraception**, je peux les développer davantage.

## Medically Approved Abortion Methods and Their Use

### Approved drugs and procedures
The evidence supports two main medically approved pathways: **medical abortion** and **surgical abortion**.

- **Medical abortion** uses **mifepristone plus misoprostol**. ACOG states this regimen is FDA-approved for use up to 70 days (or 10 weeks) of gestation, and the Cleveland Clinic notes that it can be used up through 12 weeks in some contexts [N2-R1] [N2-R3]. The WHO fact sheet also emphasizes that abortion can be safely managed using medication or surgical procedures [N1-F1]. The FDA-approved medication abortion regimen is specifically mifepristone and misoprostol, with mifepristone described as a selective progesterone receptor modulator and misoprostol as a prostaglandin E1 analogue [N2-F2].
- **Surgical abortion** is also approved and is the uterine aspiration procedure described in ACOG guidance. It is considered one of the more effective methods and allows direct assessment of pregnancy tissue by the clinician [N2-F2].

### When each method is appropriate by gestational age
The evidence is clear that gestational age limits the method chosen and the setting in which it is administered.

- **Medical abortion**: The FDA-approved regimen is explicitly for use through **10 weeks of gestation**, and ACOG’s practice bulletin is specifically for **up to 70 days (10 weeks)** of gestation [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-F2]. The ACOG document also notes that information about medication abortion after 70 days is provided in other ACOG publications, implying that care beyond 10 weeks is not covered in this specific guidance [N2-F2].
- **Surgical abortion**: The evidence does not give a specific gestational limit in the supplied materials, but ACOG’s guidance notes that uterine aspiration is most commonly used for first-trimester abortion and that the procedure is usually completed in one visit [N2-F2]. WHO’s broader abortion fact sheet emphasizes that the method must be appropriate to the pregnancy duration and that first-trimester medical abortion can be safely self-managed outside a health facility if supported by trained care [N1-F1].

### How to assess patient eligibility and contraindications
Eligibility and contraindications are a key part of clinical decision-making.

- **Eligibility**: ACOG states that most patients at 70 days of gestation or less who desire abortion are eligible for a medication abortion [N2-F2]. The guidance also notes that some patients may prefer medication abortion because of a desire to avoid procedural intervention, and it explicitly includes examples of medical conditions for which medication abortion may be preferable, such as uterine fibroids distorting the cervical canal, congenital uterine anomalies, introital scarring related to infibulation, and asthma [N2-F2]. Patients with multiple gestation pregnancies are not contraindicated; twin gestations can be treated with the same regimens as singleton gestations [N2-F2].
- **Contraindications**: ACOG clearly states that medication abortion is **not recommended** for patients with **confirmed or suspected ectopic pregnancy**, an **IUD in place** (which can be removed before medication abortion), and **current long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy** [N2-F2]. It also notes that **multiple gestation pregnancy is not a contraindication** [N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a complete list of all contraindications, but it does establish that the decision must be made with careful attention to the patient’s specific clinical situation [N2-F2].

### Additional notes from the evidence
The evidence also highlights access barriers and safety considerations. ACOG notes that the FDA currently restricts mifepristone access under a REMS program, which the guidance says does not make care safer, is not based on medical evidence or need, and creates barriers to access [N2-F2]. That context is important for understanding why clinical practice guidance may emphasize broader access and trained support even when legal restrictions exist.

## Bottom line for patient care
If you are advising a patient, the evidence supports:
- **medical abortion** for early pregnancy up to 10 weeks, with a strong emphasis on FDA-approved mifepristone plus misoprostol [N2-R1] [N2-R2] [N2-F2].
- **surgical abortion** as the other approved pathway, especially when a procedural approach is appropriate [N2-F2].
- careful assessment of **gestational age, medical history, and contraindications**, including ectopic pregnancy, IUD presence, and corticosteroid use [N2-F2].

## Legal and Ethical Framework for Safe Abortion

### Which jurisdictions permit abortion and under what conditions
The evidence here is primarily normative and guidance-oriented rather than a complete legal database, so it is important not to interpret it as a definitive list of every jurisdiction.

- **WHO’s abortion fact sheet** states that abortion is a simple health care intervention that can be safely and effectively managed by a wide range of health workers using medication or surgical procedures, appropriate to the pregnancy duration [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that **lack of access to safe, timely, affordable, and respectful abortion care is a critical public health and human rights issue** [N1-F1].
- **Center for Reproductive Rights** and **Global Abortion Policies Database** are cited as sources that map the legal status of abortion in countries and territories, with the Center for Reproductive Rights described as the “definitive record” [N1-R2] [N1-R4]. This means the actual jurisdictional boundaries are best accessed through those sources rather than the current evidence set.
- **Council on Foreign Relations** notes that **safety of abortion procedures diverges widely between countries where abortion is generally legal and countries with high restrictions** [N1-R5]. WHO also notes that **nearly all countries in the global north and central and eastern Asia currently have liberal abortion laws**, although the evidence does not list every country [N1-R3].

### What legal exceptions exist for pregnancy termination
The evidence provided does not include detailed country-specific exceptions, but it does convey the broader context that abortion laws vary significantly and that **restrictive laws can create legal risks**.

- WHO emphasizes that **restrictive abortion regulation can cause distress and stigma, and risk constituting a violation of human rights** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **regulations that force women to travel to attain legal care, or require mandatory counseling or waiting periods, can make abortion inaccessible to women with low resources** [N1-F1].
- The evidence does not provide a country-by-country listing of exceptions, so any patient-specific legal advice would need to be based on the jurisdiction in question and verified through up-to-date legal sources [N1-R2] [N1-R4].

### How to recognize legal risks when advising a patient
The evidence implies several ways legal risk can arise in clinical practice.

- **Travel requirements, waiting periods, or mandatory counseling** can impose financial and logistical burdens on patients, especially those with limited resources [N1-F1].
- **Restrictive laws** may result in **unsafe abortion**, because women may not be able to access legal services in time [N1-F1].
- **Counseling and informed consent** are central to clinical practice, but the evidence also shows that **state-developed counseling materials can be medically inaccurate** [N5-R3], which means clinicians must be especially careful in how they present information.

### How informed consent and counseling interact with legal boundaries
The evidence on informed consent and counseling is strong and directly relevant.

- **ACOG** states that patients who choose abortion should be counseled about all available methods as well as the risks, advantages, disadvantages, and different features of the options [N2-F2]. It also notes that most patients who initially are unsure about the method will have some preference after counseling [N2-F2].
- **Informed consent and shared decision-making** in obstetrics and gynecology emphasizes that an adult patient with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse treatment, including during pregnancy [N5-R1].
- **Ethical choice architecture in preabortion counseling** warns against providing emotionally charged or biased content about abortions at the time of service [N5-R2].
- **Misinformation in counseling materials** is a documented concern; a 2006 Guttmacher report found that a majority of states have enacted abortion counseling laws requiring physicians to provide specified information, and the report cautions about the medical accuracy of those materials [N5-R3].

### Bottom line for clinical practice
If you are advising a patient, the evidence supports:
- **clinical judgment** that abortion is a legal and medical intervention when carried out safely and appropriately [N1-F1].
- **jurisdictional caution**: legal access varies by country and territory, and the most accurate map of legal status is provided by the Center for Reproductive Rights and the Global Abortion Policies Database [N1-R2] [N1-R4].
- **ethical caution**: counseling should be evidence-based, non-coercive, and respectful; it should also avoid misinformation and support shared decision-making [N5-R1] [N5-R2] [N5-R3].

## Safety, Risks, and Counseling Guidance

### Complication rates and severity for each method
The evidence shows that abortion methods differ in risk profile, with medical abortion generally having a much lower complication burden than the most unsafe forms of abortion.

- **Medical abortion**: A recent systematic review of 33,846 medication abortions found an overall effectiveness rate of **96.7% for gestations up to 63 days** [N3-R1]. Another systematic review of medical abortion in the late first trimester reported complete abortion rates ranging from **78.6% to 94.6%** [N3-R2]. WHO notes that **safe abortion is very safe** when carried out using a WHO-recommended method appropriate to the pregnancy duration and by someone with the necessary skills [N1-F1].
- **Surgical abortion**: The evidence does not give a single complication rate for surgical abortion, but WHO emphasizes that **safe abortion is very safe** and that **unsafe abortion is an important preventable cause of maternal deaths and morbidities** [N1-F1]. WHO also notes that unsafe abortion can lead to **incomplete abortion, haemorrhage, infection, uterine perforation, and damage to the genital tract and internal organs** [N1-F1].
- **Systematic review of the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of abortion methods** reports that medical abortion was **95% effective**, with a continuing pregnancy rate of **0.6%** among 25,385 women [N3-R4]. The same review also states that **serious complication rates were low (0%–1%)** [N3-R3].

### Common side effects and when to seek care
The evidence describes both common and more serious adverse effects.

- **Common side effects** include **nausea and vomiting, slight irregular vaginal bleeding, fatigue, and other effects similar to oral contraceptive pills** [N4-F4]. The WHO emergency contraception fact sheet also notes that side effects are **not common, they are mild, and will normally resolve without further medications** [N4-F4].
- **When to seek care** is emphasized in counseling guidance. ACOG notes that patients should be counseled about all methods, their risks, advantages, disadvantages, and features, and that the discussion about different methods becomes clinically relevant only after the patient has considered their options and decided to have an abortion [N2-F2]. WHO’s preabortion care guidance states that patients should be provided evidence-based information on their procedure options, including clear instruction on aftercare and how to recognize potential complications requiring emergency care [N3-F3].
- **Emergency care signs** include complications such as **incomplete abortion, heavy bleeding, infection, uterine perforation, and damage to genital tract or internal organs** [N1-F1]. The evidence does not list a precise checklist, but the overall message is that patients should be taught to recognize serious symptoms and know whom to contact.

### How to counsel a patient about risks and decision-making
Counseling is a core part of safe abortion care.

- **ACOG guidance** stresses that patients who choose abortion should be counseled about all available methods as well as the risks, advantages, disadvantages, and features of these options [N2-F2]. It also notes that most patients who initially are unsure about the method will have some preference after counseling [N2-F2].
- **WHO’s preabortion care guidance** emphasizes **individualized, sensitive, and respectful communication**, **cultural sensitivity**, **review of the risks and benefits of available abortion procedures**, **options for pain management**, **support for emotional and other needs**, **confirmation that the abortion decision is voluntary**, **explanation of what will be done before, during, and after the procedure**, **description of what the patient is likely to experience**, **clear instruction on aftercare**, **how to recognize potential complications requiring emergency care**, and **information and counseling on future prevention of unintended pregnancy and contraceptive options** [N3-F3].
- **Informed consent and shared decision-making** in obstetrics and gynecology emphasizes that an adult patient with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse treatment, including during pregnancy [N5-R1]. This supports a counseling approach that respects patient autonomy while providing full disclosure.
- **Ethical choice architecture** warns against emotionally charged or biased content at the time of service, reinforcing the need for neutral, evidence-based communication [N5-R2].
- **Misinformation in counseling materials** is a documented concern, so clinicians should be especially careful to avoid inaccurate or biased counseling [N5-R3].

### Bottom line for patient counseling
If you are counseling a patient, the evidence supports:
- **clear, evidence-based information** on all available methods and their risks and benefits [N2-F2] [N3-F3].
- **respectful and patient-centered communication**, including cultural sensitivity and support for emotional needs [N3-F3].
- **shared decision-making**, so that the patient can understand and choose a method after considering their options [N5-R1].
- **warning against misinformation** and emotionally charged counseling materials [N5-R2] [N5-R3].
- **teaching patients to recognize serious complications** and know when to seek care [N1-F1] [N3-F3].

## Contraception and Emergency Contraception Comparison

### Which EC options are most effective and when they work
The evidence clearly ranks emergency contraception by effectiveness and by timing.

- **Most effective**: The **copper IUD** is the most effective type of emergency contraception [N4-R1] [N4-R5]. WHO also states that emergency contraception can prevent **up to over 95% of pregnancies when taken within 5 days** after intercourse [N4-R4]. The copper IUD works as well on day 1 as on day 5 [N4-R5].
- **Next most effective**: **Ulipristal acetate (UPA)** is also highly effective [N4-R1] [N4-R4]. WHO recommends ECPs with UPA, and notes that they are more effective between **72–120 hours** after unprotected intercourse than other ECPs [N4-F4].
- **Levonorgestrel pills** are also effective, but less so than the copper IUD and UPA [N4-R1] [N4-R4]. WHO says ECPs with LNG had a pregnancy rate of **1.2% to 2.1%** [N4-F4].
- **Combined oral contraceptive pills** are also an option, but WHO says they are less effective than ECPs with UPA or LNG [N4-F4].

### How EC differs from abortion and when it should be used
The evidence makes this distinction explicit.

- **Emergency contraception does not induce an abortion**. WHO states that EC cannot interrupt an established pregnancy or harm a developing embryo [N4-F4]. ACOG also notes that emergency contraception pills prevent pregnancy by preventing or delaying ovulation and do not induce an abortion [N4-F4].
- **EC should be used after unprotected sex** when pregnancy is not yet established. WHO lists several situations where EC can be used, including when no contraceptive has been used, sexual assault, or contraceptive failure [N4-F4].
- **EC is not appropriate after implantation of a fertilized egg**. The evidence does not give a specific implantation timeline, but WHO’s wording is explicit: EC works to prevent pregnancy and does not interrupt an established pregnancy [N4-F4].

### Contraceptive options to discuss after a pregnancy loss or abortion
The evidence supports immediate postabortion contraceptive counseling and highlights several methods.

- **All contraceptive methods are safe and effective when provided immediately after abortion procedures and when otherwise medically appropriate for a patient** [N6-R2]. ACOG similarly states that all contraceptive methods are safe and effective when initiated immediately after abortion [N6-R1].
- **Contraceptive counseling for postabortion patients** should review contraceptive preferences, efficacy, and convenience [N6-R3]. UpToDate notes that postabortion contraception is significantly more effective in preventing repeat unintended pregnancy and abortion when it is provided before women leave the facility [N6-R4].
- **Immediate postabortion options** include a wide range of methods, including **hormonal contraception, IUDs, implants, and other reversible methods**. The evidence does not list every method, but it does establish that counseling should be tailored to the patient’s preferences and that **no additional contraceptive protection is needed after a copper IUD** [N4-F4] [N6-R2].
- **Timing of effectiveness**: Combined hormonal contraceptives take one week to be fully effective, as do the Skyla and Kyleena IUDs; the implant takes 4 days; and other methods vary [N6-R5]. This is important because it affects when patients can safely resume sexual activity without risk of another unintended pregnancy.

### Bottom line for clinical practice
If you are advising a patient, the evidence supports:
- **copper IUD as the most effective emergency contraception** [N4-R1] [N4-R5].
- **ulipristal acetate as a highly effective alternative**, especially between 72–120 hours after unprotected intercourse [N4-R1] [N4-F4].
- **levonorgestrel pills as effective, but less so than the IUD and UPA** [N4-R1] [N4-F4].
- **EC is not abortion**, and should be used when pregnancy is not yet established [N4-F4].
- **postabortion counseling should begin immediately**, with immediate access to effective contraceptive methods [N6-R1] [N6-R2].
- **counseling should be patient-centered, including preferences, efficacy, and timing of effectiveness** [N6-R3] [N6-R5].
